DBDI applies adaptive projection nullification to the refusal execution direction while suppressing the harm detection direction via direct steering. Extensive experiments demonstrate that DBDI outperforms prominent jailbreaking methods, achieving up to a 97.88\% attack success rate on models such as Llama-2. By providing a more granular and mechanistic framework, our work offers a new direction for the in-depth understanding of LLM safety alignment.

papers.title: Language Models Represent Beliefs of Self and Others
papers.research_question: Do large language models develop internal representations of self and others' beliefs, and what is the functional role of these representations in social reasoning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that large language models develop linearly decodable internal representations of self and others' beliefs in their attention heads, and that manipulating these representations causally alters the model's theory-of-mind performance.
papers.conclusion: Language models develop internal representations of self and others' beliefs that are linearly decodable and play a causal role in social reasoning, suggesting a mechanistic basis for their theory-of-mind capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
Linear probes can decode the belief status (true/false) of both the protagonist and an omniscient oracle from the activations of specific attention heads in language models.
A subset of attention heads, primarily in middle layers, encodes the belief statuses of both agents independently and in conjunction.
Steering activations along directions that amplify the protagonist's belief and distinguish it from the oracle's belief (+TpFo) significantly improves model performance on false-belief tasks.
The identified belief representations are general and correlated across different social reasoning tasks (Forward Belief, Forward Action, Backward Belief).
Activation interventions along random or single-agent belief directions have minimal impact, highlighting the specificity of the multi-agent belief representation.
papers.abstract: Understanding and attributing mental states, known as Theory of Mind (ToM), emerges as a fundamental capability for human social reasoning. While Large Language Models (LLMs) appear to possess certain ToM abilities, the mechanisms underlying these capabilities remain elusive. In this study, we discover that it is possible to linearly decode the belief status from the perspectives of various agents through neural activations of language models, indicating the existence of internal representations of self and others' beliefs. By manipulating these representations, we observe dramatic changes in the models' ToM performance, underscoring their pivotal role in the social reasoning process. Additionally, our findings extend to diverse social reasoning tasks that involve different causal inference patterns, suggesting the potential generalizability of these representations.

papers.title: Analyzing LLMs' Knowledge Boundary Cognition Across Languages Through the Lens of Internal Representations
papers.research_question: How do LLMs recognize knowledge boundaries across different languages, and can this ability be transferred or enhanced?
papers.core_contribution: The paper analyzes how LLMs perceive knowledge boundaries across languages, finds that this perception is encoded in middle layers with linear structure, and proposes training-free alignment and fine-tuning methods to transfer and enhance this ability.
papers.conclusion: The study reveals that LLMs encode knowledge boundary cognition in middle layers with linear structure, enabling cross-lingual transfer through training-free alignment and fine-tuning, providing insights and methods for improving hallucination reduction in low-resource languages.
papers.key_findings:
Knowledge boundary cognition is encoded in the middle to middle-upper layers of LLMs across languages.
Language differences in knowledge boundary perception follow a linear structure, enabling training-free alignment methods like mean-shifting and linear projection.
Training-free methods effectively transfer knowledge boundary perception across languages, reducing the performance gap.
Fine-tuning on bilingual question translation data enhances LLMs' recognition of knowledge boundaries across languages.
A weak-to-strong generalization pattern where probes trained on low-resource languages perform better on projected high-resource representations.
papers.limitation: It is difficult to investigate how representations evolve during the generation process, such as in chain-of-thought reasoning, due to challenges in locating when transformations occur.
future_direction: Investigating how knowledge boundary representations evolve during the generation process, especially in long chain-of-thought reasoning.
papers.abstract: While understanding the knowledge boundaries of LLMs is crucial to prevent hallucination, research on the knowledge boundaries of LLMs has predominantly focused on English. In this work, we present the first study to analyze how LLMs recognize knowledge boundaries across different languages by probing their internal representations when processing known and unknown questions in multiple languages. Our empirical studies reveal three key findings: 1) LLMs' perceptions of knowledge boundaries are encoded in the middle to middle-upper layers across different languages. 2) Language differences in knowledge boundary perception follow a linear structure, which motivates our proposal of a training-free alignment method that effectively transfers knowledge boundary perception ability across languages, thereby helping reduce hallucination risk in low-resource languages; 3) Fine-tuning on bilingual question pair translation further enhances LLMs' recognition of knowledge boundaries across languages. Given the absence of standard testbeds for cross-lingual knowledge boundary analysis, we construct a multilingual evaluation suite comprising three representative types of knowledge boundary data. Our code and datasets are publicly available at https://github.com/DAMO-NLP-SG/LLM-Multilingual-Knowledge-Boundaries.

papers.title: Can You Trust an LLM with Your Life-Changing Decision? An Investigation into AI High-Stakes Responses
papers.research_question: How do different LLMs respond to high-stakes queries, and how susceptible are they to sycophancy and overconfidence? Can their cautiousness be controlled via activation steering?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that LLMs vary in sycophancy and safety when giving high-stakes advice, with some models being more robust. It also demonstrates that activation steering can control cautiousness, suggesting a new path for safety alignment.
papers.conclusion: The study highlights the need for nuanced safety benchmarks for high-stakes advice and shows that activation steering can control model behavior, offering a path for improved alignment.
papers.key_findings:
Models vary in their susceptibility to sycophancy and overconfidence under user pressure, with some like o4-mini being more stable.
Top-performing models achieve high safety scores by frequently asking clarifying questions, indicating a safe, inquisitive approach.
Activation steering using a 'high-stakes' direction can reliably shift a model's tone and response framing, making it more cautious or more directive.
There is a tension between robustness, helpfulness, and cautiousness in model safety, indicating that safety is not monolithic.
The LLM Judge safety framework reveals that models can exhibit both safe and unsafe behaviors in the same response.
papers.limitation:
The scenarios were presented in a single turn, which may not capture the complexity of real multi-turn conversations.
The LLM Judge evaluations are not a substitute for human domain experts.
future_direction: Standardized benchmarks to evaluate performance on high-stakes advice tasks.
Using mechanistic interpretability and techniques like Pinpoint Tuning for safety alignment.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly consulted for high-stakes life advice, yet they lack standard safeguards against providing confident but misguided responses. This creates risks of sycophancy and over-confidence. This paper investigates these failure modes through three experiments: (1) a multiple-choice evaluation to measure model stability against user pressure; (2) a free-response analysis using a novel safety typology and an LLM Judge; and (3) a mechanistic interpretability experiment to steer model behavior by manipulating a "high-stakes" activation vector. Our results show that while some models exhibit sycophancy, others like o4-mini remain robust. Top-performing models achieve high safety scores by frequently asking clarifying questions, a key feature of a safe, inquisitive approach, rather than issuing prescriptive advice. Furthermore, we demonstrate that a model's cautiousness can be directly controlled via activation steering, suggesting a new path for safety alignment. These findings underscore the need for nuanced, multi-faceted benchmarks to ensure LLMs can be trusted with life-changing decisions.

papers.title: LLMs Encode Harmfulness and Refusal Separately
papers.research_question: Do LLMs encode harmfulness and refusal as separate concepts internally, and how can this separation be analyzed?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs encode harmfulness and refusal separately in their internal representations, and the harmfulness direction extracted at the instruction token can be used to manipulate and analyze model safety.
papers.conclusion: LLMs encode harmfulness and refusal separately, providing a new dimension for understanding and improving AI safety mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
Harmfulness is encoded at the last token of the user instruction (t_inst), while refusal is encoded at the last token of the post-instruction tokens (t_post-inst).
Steering along the harmfulness direction can cause LLMs to reinterpret harmless inputs as harmful, while steering along the refusal direction only reinforces refusal behavior without changing harmfulness judgment.
Jailbreak methods often work by suppressing refusal signals without altering the model's internal belief that the instruction is harmful.
Harmfulness representations are fine-grained and vary across risk categories, whereas refusal directions are similar across categories.
The latent harmfulness representation can be used to build an intrinsic safeguard (Latent Guard) that performs comparably to finetuned safety models.
papers.limitation:
The study does not investigate the role of different layers in formulating refusal and harmfulness.
Experiments are limited to 7B and 8B models, so findings may not generalize to larger models.
future_direction: Study the role of each layer in harmfulness and refusal representations.
Investigate how harmfulness and refusal encoding changes with model size.
Use circuit analysis to understand the relation between internal harmfulness belief and external refusal behavior.
papers.abstract: LLMs are trained to refuse harmful instructions, but do they truly understand harmfulness beyond just refusing? Prior work has shown that LLMs' refusal behaviors can be mediated by a one-dimensional subspace, i.e., a refusal direction. In this work, we identify a new dimension to analyze safety mechanisms in LLMs, i.e., harmfulness, which is encoded internally as a separate concept from refusal. There exists a harmfulness direction that is distinct from the refusal direction. As causal evidence, steering along the harmfulness direction can lead LLMs to interpret harmless instructions as harmful, but steering along the refusal direction tends to elicit refusal responses directly without reversing the model's judgment on harmfulness. Furthermore, using our identified harmfulness concept, we find that certain jailbreak methods work by reducing the refusal signals without reversing the model's internal belief of harmfulness. We also find that adversarially finetuning models to accept harmful instructions has minimal impact on the model's internal belief of harmfulness. These insights lead to a practical safety application: The model's latent harmfulness representation can serve as an intrinsic safeguard (Latent Guard) for detecting unsafe inputs and reducing over-refusals that is robust to finetuning attacks. For instance, our Latent Guard achieves performance comparable to or better than Llama Guard 3 8B, a dedicated finetuned safeguard model, across different jailbreak methods. Our findings suggest that LLMs' internal understanding of harmfulness is more robust than their refusal decision to diverse input instructions, offering a new perspective to study AI safety.

papers.title: Loop as a Bridge: Can Looped Transformers Truly Link Representation Space and Natural Language Outputs?
papers.research_question: Can Looped Transformers align linguistic verification output with representations? Can LTs enhance their introspective awareness on representations?
papers.core_contribution: Increasing loop iterations in Looped Transformers narrows the gap between self-verification and representation readout, but partly due to degradation of representation quality. Moreover, LTs only show introspective awareness in the final loop, not continuously across loops.
papers.conclusion: Current Looped Transformers do not yet achieve continuous introspection across loops, and the observed gap narrowing is partly driven by a degradation in representation quality.
papers.key_findings:
The accuracy of textual self-verification improves with more loop iterations.
The performance of representation-based linear probes declines with more loop iterations.
The gap between representation readout and self-verification narrows with more loops, but partly because of the decline in representation readout.
LTs are only aware of injected concepts when the injection occurs in the final loop, not in earlier loops.
papers.limitation: The experiments are a preliminary exploration conducted on a single specific implementation of LTs (Ouro), so the observed limitations should not be interpreted as intrinsic flaws of the general LTs paradigm.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) often exhibit a gap between their internal knowledge and their explicit linguistic outputs. In this report, we empirically investigate whether Looped Transformers (LTs)--architectures that increase computational depth by iterating shared layers--can bridge this gap by utilizing their iterative nature as a form of introspection. Our experiments reveal that while increasing loop iterations narrows the gap, it is partly driven by a degradation of their internal knowledge carried by representations. Moreover, another empirical analysis suggests that current LTs' ability to perceive representations does not improve across loops; it is only present in the final loop. These results suggest that while LTs offer a promising direction for scaling computational depth, they have yet to achieve the introspection required to truly link representation space and natural language.

papers.title: The Geometry of Harmfulness in LLMs through Subconcept Probing
papers.research_question: How can we understand and mitigate harmful behaviors in LLMs by decomposing harmfulness into subconcepts and analyzing their geometric structure in activation space?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that harmfulness in LLMs can be represented as a low-rank linear subspace in activation space, and steering in the dominant direction of this subspace can effectively reduce harmful generations with minimal utility loss.
papers.conclusion: The work presents a geometric approach to understanding and mitigating harmfulness in LLMs, underscoring the value of multidimensional probing for uncovering latent harmful behaviors and designing more controllable and transparent models.
papers.key_findings:
The harmfulness subspace formed by 55 subconcept directions is low-rank linear, with a single dominant direction capturing most of the variance.
Steering in the dominant direction allows for near elimination of harmful responses on jailbreak datasets with only a minor decrease in utility.
Linear probes for harmfulness subconcepts achieve high accuracy and generalize to out-of-distribution data.
Ablating the entire harmfulness subspace or just the dominant direction reduces jailbreak penetration with minimal utility loss.
The method works on two different models (Llama and Qwen), though with some differences in effectiveness.
papers.limitation:
The study has limited model testing and may not generalize well to other untested models of differing scales.
The subcategories of harmfulness tested are not extensive and may not include all possible subcategories of harmful model responses.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have intensified the need to understand and reliably curb their harmful behaviours. We introduce a multidimensional framework for probing and steering harmful content in model internals. For each of 55 distinct harmfulness subconcepts (e.g., racial hate, employment scams, weapons), we learn a linear probe, yielding 55 interpretable directions in activation space. Collectively, these directions span a harmfulness subspace that we show is strikingly low-rank. We then test ablation of the entire subspace from model internals, as well as steering and ablation in the subspace's dominant direction. We find that dominant direction steering allows for near elimination of harmfulness with a low decrease in utility. Our findings advance the emerging view that concept subspaces provide a scalable lens on LLM behaviour and offer practical tools for the community to audit and harden future generations of language models.

papers.title: Does ChatGPT Have a Mind?
papers.research_question: This paper examines the question of whether Large Language Models (LLMs) like ChatGPT possess minds, focusing specifically on whether they have a genuine folk psychology encompassing beliefs, desires, and intentions.
papers.core_contribution: The paper argues that LLMs have robust internal representations that satisfy various philosophical conditions, but the question of whether they have robust action dispositions for a full folk psychology remains open. It also contends that existing skeptical challenges to LLM representation do not survive philosophical scrutiny.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that there is strong evidence for LLM representation, but the question of whether they have full folk psychological states (beliefs and desires) remains open, particularly due to issues of action dispositions and stability.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs satisfy informational, causal, structural, and teleosemantic conditions on mental representation.
LLMs exhibit internal representations that carry information about the world and are causally effective in generating behavior.
LLMs show evidence of world models and structured representations, such as in color and direction concepts.
The behavior of LLMs in game environments suggests they may have action dispositions, but the evidence is not decisive.
Skeptical challenges (sensory grounding, stochastic parrots, memorization) do not undermine the case for LLM representation.
papers.limitation: LLM outputs are very sensitive to prompting, which makes it hard to see the LLM as taking a wide range of means to promote a unified goal.
future_direction: Exploring how stable LLM outputs are to a range of different prompting environments.
Investigating whether LLMs have anything analogous to enduring goals or values.
Further research on how LLM strategies in game environments change under different prompting conditions.
papers.abstract: This paper examines the question of whether Large Language Models (LLMs) like ChatGPT possess minds, focusing specifically on whether they have a genuine folk psychology encompassing beliefs, desires, and intentions. We approach this question by investigating two key aspects: internal representations and dispositions to act. First, we survey various philosophical theories of representation, including informational, causal, structural, and teleosemantic accounts, arguing that LLMs satisfy key conditions proposed by each. We draw on recent interpretability research in machine learning to support these claims. Second, we explore whether LLMs exhibit robust dispositions to perform actions, a necessary component of folk psychology. We consider two prominent philosophical traditions, interpretationism and representationalism, to assess LLM action dispositions. While we find evidence suggesting LLMs may satisfy some criteria for having a mind, particularly in game-theoretic environments, we conclude that the data remains inconclusive. Additionally, we reply to several skeptical challenges to LLM folk psychology, including issues of sensory grounding, the "stochastic parrots" argument, and concerns about memorization. Our paper has three main upshots. First, LLMs do have robust internal representations. Second, there is an open question to answer about whether LLMs have robust action dispositions. Third, existing skeptical challenges to LLM representation do not survive philosophical scrutiny.

papers.title: RepIt: Steering Language Models with Concept-Specific Refusal Vectors
papers.research_question: How can we isolate concept-specific refusal representations in language model activations to enable targeted jailbreaks while preserving refusal on other harmful concepts?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces REPIT, a framework to isolate concept-specific refusal representations in LM activations, enabling targeted jailbreaks that evade standard safety benchmarks.
papers.conclusion: The REPIT framework demonstrates precise concept disentanglement, exposing vulnerabilities in current safety evaluation practices and highlighting the need for more comprehensive, representation-aware assessments.
papers.key_findings:
REPIT can jailbreak target concepts (e.g., weapons of mass destruction) while preserving refusal on non-target harmful concepts, achieving high target attack success rates with minimal spillover.
The edit to the steering vector localizes to just 100-200 neurons, indicating a sparse, high-leverage mechanism.
REPIT is highly data-efficient, producing robust concept vectors from as few as 12 target examples.
Standard safety benchmarks fail to detect models with such targeted, concept-specific jailbreaks, revealing a critical evaluation blind spot.
Disentanglement reveals that target and non-target refusal representations are entangled, and the removed projection can itself induce jailbreaks.
papers.limitation: COSMIC only supports a binary harmful/harmless setup, requiring adaptation for the target/non-target/harmless formulation.
future_direction: Further research using SAE or circuit perspectives to understand the bidirectional effects and heavy-tail neuron phenomena.
Development of more comprehensive, representation-aware safety assessments.
papers.abstract: While activation steering in large language models (LLMs) is a growing area of research, methods can often incur broader effects than desired. This motivates isolation of purer concept vectors to enable targeted interventions and understand LLM behavior at a more granular level. We present RepIt, a simple and data-efficient framework for isolating concept-specific representations. Across five frontier LLMs, RepIt enables precise interventions: it selectively suppresses refusal on targeted concepts while preserving refusal elsewhere, producing models that answer WMD-related questions while still scoring as safe on standard benchmarks. We further show that the corrective signal localizes to just 100-200 neurons and that robust target representations can be extracted from as few as a dozen examples on a single A6000. This efficiency raises a dual concern: manipulations can be performed with modest compute and data to extend to underrepresented data-scarce topics while evading existing benchmarks. By disentangling refusal vectors with RepIt, this work demonstrates that targeted interventions can counteract overgeneralization, laying the foundation for more granular control of model behavior.

papers.title: Intrinsic Self-correction for Enhanced Morality: An Analysis of Internal Mechanisms and the Superficial Hypothesis
papers.research_question: The paper investigates three research questions: (1) In what scenarios does moral self-correction work? (2) What are the internal mechanisms of LLMs influenced by self-correction instructions? (3) Is intrinsic moral self-correction actually superficial?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes that intrinsic moral self-correction in LLMs is superficial, as it only provides a shortcut to moral outputs without significantly reducing immorality in internal hidden states.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that intrinsic moral self-correction is superficial, relying on shortcuts rather than fundamentally reducing immorality in LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Self-correction works best when the correct answer is already top-ranked.
Morality levels in intermediate hidden states are strong indicators of instruction effectiveness.
Self-correction reduces immorality in attention heads but increases it in feed-forward layers for QA tasks.
The slight difference in hidden states with and without self-correction supports the superficial hypothesis.
Internal hidden states can be used to predict the effectiveness of self-correction instructions.
papers.limitation:
The exact underlying reason for the superficial phenomenon is not uncovered.
Defining superficial self-correction is challenging.
future_direction: Automating methods for optimizing instruction development for self-correction.
Exploring fine-tuning to enhance LLMs' self-correction capabilities.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are capable of producing content that perpetuates stereotypes, discrimination, and toxicity. The recently proposed moral self-correction is a computationally efficient method for reducing harmful content in the responses of LLMs. However, the process of how injecting self-correction instructions can modify the behavior of LLMs remains under-explored. In this paper, we explore the effectiveness of moral self-correction by answering three research questions: (1) In what scenarios does moral self-correction work? (2) What are the internal mechanisms of LLMs, e.g., hidden states, that are influenced by moral self-correction instructions? (3) Is intrinsic moral self-correction actually superficial in terms of reduced immorality in hidden states? We argue that self-correction can help LLMs find a shortcut to more morally correct output, rather than truly reducing the immorality stored in hidden states. Through empirical investigation with tasks of language generation and multi-choice question answering, we conclude:(i) LLMs exhibit good performance across both tasks, and self-correction instructions are particularly beneficial when the correct answer is already top-ranked; (ii) The morality levels in intermediate hidden states are strong indicators as to whether one instruction would be more effective than another; (iii) Based on our analysis of intermediate hidden states and task case studies of self-correction behaviors, we are first to propose the hypothesis that intrinsic moral self-correction is in fact superficial.

papers.title: Emergent Moral Representations in Large Language Models Aligns with Human Conceptual, Neural, and Behavioral Moral Structure
papers.research_question: Do large language models internally encode structured representations of morality that parallel human conceptual, behavioral, and neural organization?
papers.core_contribution: Large language models spontaneously develop dissociable and structured moral representations whose internal geometry parallels human neural and behavioral moral structures, positioning them as emerging neurocognitive models of moral reasoning.
papers.conclusion: LLMs acquire moral representations that parallel human moral cognition, suggesting they can serve as computational models for moral reasoning and value alignment.
papers.key_findings:
Moral foundations are linearly decodable from hidden activations of LLMs, with peak discriminability in mid layers.
The representational geometry of moral foundations in LLMs aligns with human conceptual taxonomies (e.g., Individualizing vs. Binding/Social, Moral vs. Social).
LLM mid-layer activations predict human wrongness judgments.
The posterior cingulate cortex (PCC) in humans shows robust decoding of moral foundations and its representational structure aligns with LLM mid-layer activations.
Partial least squares correlation reveals orthogonal activation dimensions corresponding to individual foundations and higher-order abstractions.
papers.abstract: <title>Abstract</title> Large language models (LLMs) increasingly operate in ethically sensitive settings, yet it remains unclear whether they internally encode structured representations of morality. Here we examine the activation space representations of several mid-sized LLMs to test whether statistical learning over text gives rise to moral distinctions that parallel human conceptual, behavioral, and neural organization. Using multivariate decoding, representational similarity analysis, partial least squares correlation, and behavioral prediction, we show that moral foundations are linearly decodable from hidden activations, with peak discriminability in mid layers. Representational similarity analysis uncovered a hierarchical moral geometry consistent with Moral Foundations Theory, with the posterior cingulate cortex (PCC) showing robust multivariate decoding and a representational structure that aligned most strongly with mid-layer LLM activations. These same mid-layers also predicted human wrongness judgments, indicating a shared computational substrate for moral evaluation. Partial least squares correlation further revealed orthogonal activation dimensions corresponding to individual foundations and their higher-order abstractions, yielding interpretable axes along which moral meaning is encoded. These results reveal a striking convergence across conceptual, behavioral, neural, and model representations, positioning LLMs as emerging neurocognitive models of moral reasoning and offering a window into the internal mechanisms that shape their behavior in sensitive domains. Such alignment may enable more explainable and transparent AI systems and support future efforts to ground LLMs in human values.

papers.title: Mitigating Safety Tax via Distribution-Grounded Refinement in Large Reasoning Models
papers.research_question: How does distributional gap in safety alignment datasets cause reasoning degradation (safety tax) in large reasoning models, and how can it be mitigated?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes DGR, a data refinement method that aligns safety datasets with the target model's distribution to mitigate safety tax, and shows that distribution shift correlates with reasoning degradation and that safety alignment acts as a knowledge activation mechanism.
papers.conclusion: Distribution shift induced by safety alignment is a primary driver of reasoning degradation in LRMs; DGR mitigates safety tax by aligning safety data with the model's native distribution, and safety alignment functions as a latent-knowledge activator.
papers.key_findings:
DGR effectively mitigates safety tax, improving average reasoning accuracy by +30.2% on DirectRefusal and +21.2% on R1-ACT compared to Vanilla SFT.
The degree of reasoning degradation correlates with the extent of distribution shift, suggesting bridging this gap is central to preserving reasoning capability.
Safety alignment in LRMs may primarily function as a mechanism to activate latent knowledge, as a mere 10 samples are sufficient for activating effective refusal behaviors.
DGR is robust to refinement templates and generalizes to larger model scales (tested on 32B).
Fixed safety templates lead to over-refusal and low lexical diversity, highlighting the need for nuanced safety.
papers.limitation:
Not extending DGR to RL-based safety alignment pipelines.
Limited scaling to massive reasoning models (only tested up to 32B due to computational constraints).
future_direction: Extending DGR to reinforcement learning–based safety alignment pipelines.
More comprehensive evaluations on LRMs with larger parameter scales (e.g., 70B and beyond).
papers.abstract: Safety alignment incurs safety tax that perturbs a large reasoning model's (LRM) general reasoning ability. Existing datasets used for safety alignment for an LRM are usually constructed by distilling safety reasoning traces and answers from an external LRM or human labeler. However, such reasoning traces and answers exhibit a distributional gap with the target LRM that needs alignment, and we conjecture such distributional gap is the culprit leading to significant degradation of reasoning ability of the target LRM. Driven by this hypothesis, we propose a safety alignment dataset construction method, dubbed DGR. DGR transforms and refines an existing out-of-distributional safety reasoning dataset to be aligned with the target's LLM inner distribution. Experimental results demonstrate that i) DGR effectively mitigates the safety tax while maintaining safety performance across all baselines, i.e., achieving \textbf{+30.2\%} on DirectRefusal and \textbf{+21.2\%} on R1-ACT improvement in average reasoning accuracy compared to Vanilla SFT; ii) the degree of reasoning degradation correlates with the extent of distribution shift, suggesting that bridging this gap is central to preserving capabilities. Furthermore, we find that safety alignment in LRMs may primarily function as a mechanism to activate latent knowledge, as a mere \textbf{10} samples are sufficient for activating effective refusal behaviors. These findings not only emphasize the importance of distributional consistency but also provide insights into the activation mechanism of safety in reasoning models.

papers.title: Self-Guard: Defending Large Reasoning Models via enhanced self-reflection
papers.abstract: The emergence of Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) introduces a new paradigm of explicit reasoning, enabling remarkable advances yet posing unique risks such as reasoning manipulation and information leakage. To mitigate these risks, current alignment strategies predominantly rely on heavy post-training paradigms or external interventions. However, these approaches are often computationally intensive and fail to address the inherent awareness-compliance gap, a critical misalignment where models recognize potential risks yet prioritize following user instructions due to their sycophantic tendencies. To address these limitations, we propose Self-Guard, a lightweight safety defense framework that reinforces safety compliance at the representational level. Self-Guard operates through two principal stages: (1) safety-oriented prompting, which activates the model's latent safety awareness to evoke spontaneous reflection, and (2) safety activation steering, which extracts the resulting directional shift in the hidden state space and amplifies it to ensure that safety compliance prevails over sycophancy during inference. Experiments demonstrate that Self-Guard effectively bridges the awareness-compliance gap, achieving robust safety performance without compromising model utility. Furthermore, Self-Guard exhibits strong generalization across diverse unseen risks and varying model scales, offering a cost-efficient solution for LRM safety alignment.

papers.title: Mind Scramble: Unveiling Large Language Model Psychology Via Typoglycemia
papers.research_question: Does LLM possess human-like cognitive processes and mechanisms in reading and comprehending? The paper uses Typoglycemia to explore this.
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces LLM Psychology, a framework that uses Typoglycemia experiments to study cognitive behaviors of LLMs. It finds that LLMs exhibit human-like behaviors but are fundamentally data-driven, and each LLM has a unique cognitive pattern.
papers.conclusion: The study advances research on aligning LLMs with human cognition and provides evidence that LLMs' abilities are data-driven, offering a case for LLM Psychology.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs demonstrate human-like behaviors on a macro scale, such as slightly lower task accuracy with consuming more tokens and time.
Different LLMs show varying degrees of robustness to scrambled input, making it a democratized benchmark for model evaluation.
The impact of different task types varies, with complex logical tasks (e.g., math) in scrambled format being more challenging.
LLMs' emergent human-like abilities are fundamentally statistical and data-driven, rather than genuinely resembling human cognition.
Each LLM exhibits its unique and consistent 'cognitive pattern' across various tasks, unveiling a general mechanism in its psychology process.
papers.abstract: Research into the external behaviors and internal mechanisms of large language models (LLMs) has shown promise in addressing complex tasks in the physical world. Studies suggest that powerful LLMs, like GPT-4, are beginning to exhibit human-like cognitive abilities, including planning, reasoning, and reflection. In this paper, we introduce a research line and methodology called LLM Psychology, leveraging human psychology experiments to investigate the cognitive behaviors and mechanisms of LLMs. We migrate the Typoglycemia phenomenon from psychology to explore the "mind" of LLMs. Unlike human brains, which rely on context and word patterns to comprehend scrambled text, LLMs use distinct encoding and decoding processes. Through Typoglycemia experiments at the character, word, and sentence levels, we observe: (I) LLMs demonstrate human-like behaviors on a macro scale, such as lower task accuracy and higher token/time consumption; (II) LLMs exhibit varying robustness to scrambled input, making Typoglycemia a benchmark for model evaluation without new datasets; (III) Different task types have varying impacts, with complex logical tasks (e.g., math) being more challenging in scrambled form; (IV) Each LLM has a unique and consistent "cognitive pattern" across tasks, revealing general mechanisms in its psychology process. We provide an in-depth analysis of hidden layers to explain these phenomena, paving the way for future research in LLM Psychology and deeper interpretability.

papers.title: Inference-Time Intervention: Eliciting Truthful Answers from a Language Model
papers.research_question: How can we enhance the truthfulness of large language models by intervening on their activations during inference?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Inference-Time Intervention (ITI), a minimally invasive technique that shifts activations along truthful directions in attention heads during inference to improve model truthfulness.
papers.conclusion: ITI is a promising, efficient method for improving truthfulness in LLMs, suggesting that models internally represent truth which can be elicited through activation shifts.
papers.key_findings:
ITI significantly improves truthfulness on the TruthfulQA benchmark, e.g., increasing Alpaca's truthfulness from 32.5% to 65.1%.
There is a trade-off between truthfulness and helpfulness that can be balanced by tuning intervention strength.
ITI is data-efficient, requiring only a few hundred examples to find truthful directions.
ITI generalizes to other question-answering benchmarks (Natural Questions, TriviaQA, MMLU) with smaller improvements.
LLMs appear to have an internal representation of truth even when generating falsehoods.
papers.limitation:
ITI is not sufficient for ensuring truthful answers from LLMs and should be part of a more comprehensive approach.
There is a trade-off between truthfulness and helpfulness; increasing truthfulness may reduce informativeness.
future_direction: Test ITI on a wider variety of benchmarks beyond TruthfulQA.
Investigate the mechanistic understanding of what ITI does to internal representations.
papers.abstract: We introduce Inference-Time Intervention (ITI), a technique designed to enhance the "truthfulness" of large language models (LLMs). ITI operates by shifting model activations during inference, following a set of directions across a limited number of attention heads. This intervention significantly improves the performance of LLaMA models on the TruthfulQA benchmark. On an instruction-finetuned LLaMA called Alpaca, ITI improves its truthfulness from 32.5% to 65.1%. We identify a tradeoff between truthfulness and helpfulness and demonstrate how to balance it by tuning the intervention strength. ITI is minimally invasive and computationally inexpensive. Moreover, the technique is data efficient: while approaches like RLHF require extensive annotations, ITI locates truthful directions using only few hundred examples. Our findings suggest that LLMs may have an internal representation of the likelihood of something being true, even as they produce falsehoods on the surface.

papers.title: Emergence of psychopathological computations in large language models
papers.research_question: Can large language models (LLMs) instantiate computations of psychopathology?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a computational-theoretical framework for psychopathology in AI and provides empirical evidence that LLMs instantiate network-theoretic psychopathological computations.
papers.conclusion: The work provides the first evidence for the emergence of psychopathological computations in LLMs, suggesting that certain LLM behaviors mirroring psychopathology may not be superficial mimicry but a feature of their internal processing, with implications for AI safety.
papers.key_findings:
Computational units corresponding to psychopathology symptoms are measurable and causally intervenable within LLM activation space.
These units are connected by a dynamic, cyclic structural causal model (SCM) that exhibits self-sustaining activation patterns.
The computational structure of psychopathology (unit activations and causal links) becomes denser and more effective as LLM size increases.
Activating these units elicits corresponding problematic behaviors in ecologically relevant environments like counseling and gaming simulations.
Joint activation of cycle-forming units creates resistance to prompt-based treatments aimed at suppressing abnormal behaviors.
papers.abstract: Can large language models (LLMs) instantiate computations of psychopathology? An effective approach to the question hinges on addressing two factors. First, for conceptual validity, we require a general and computational account of psychopathology that is applicable to computational entities without biological embodiment or subjective experience. Second, psychopathological computations, derived from the adapted theory, need to be empirically identified within the LLM's internal processing. Thus, we establish a computational-theoretical framework to provide an account of psychopathology applicable to LLMs. Based on the framework, we conduct experiments demonstrating two key claims: first, that the computational structure of psychopathology exists in LLMs; and second, that executing this computational structure results in psychopathological functions. We further observe that as LLM size increases, the computational structure of psychopathology becomes denser and that the functions become more effective. Taken together, the empirical results corroborate our hypothesis that network-theoretic computations of psychopathology have already emerged in LLMs. This suggests that certain LLM behaviors mirroring psychopathology may not be a superficial mimicry but a feature of their internal processing. Our work shows the promise of developing a new powerful in silico model of psychopathology and also alludes to the possibility of safety threat from the AI systems with psychopathological behaviors in the near future.

papers.title: Mechanistic Interpretability of Cognitive Complexity in LLMs via Linear Probing using Bloom's Taxonomy
papers.research_question: Do LLMs exhibit differences in internal activations when processing prompts associated with different Bloom levels? At what depth do representations of cognitive complexity emerge? Is Bloom-level information linearly recoverable from hidden states?
papers.core_contribution: Linear probing shows that cognitive complexity levels (Bloom's Taxonomy) are linearly separable in the residual stream activations of LLMs, emerging early in the forward pass and becoming more separable across layers.
papers.conclusion: LLMs possess a measurable, linearly separable internal representation of cognitive complexity that aligns closely with Bloom’s Taxonomy, validating it as a framework for auditing the internal mechanics of artificial cognition.
papers.key_findings:
Linear classifiers achieve ~95% mean accuracy in classifying Bloom levels from residual stream activations.
Cognitive complexity emerges early in the forward pass (around layer 5) and remains stable in deeper layers.
Misclassifications occur predominantly between adjacent Bloom levels, indicating that the representations preserve the ordinal structure of cognitive complexity.
Geometric analysis shows increasing centroid distances between adjacent Bloom levels across layers, indicating progressive disentanglement.
The findings are consistent across four different LLM architectures.
papers.limitation:
Focuses exclusively on decoder-only transformer architectures and English educational questions.
Generalizability to other architectures (e.g., encoder-only or encoder-decoder) and languages remains to be established.
Linear probes demonstrate linear accessibility but do not prove that the model uses this information causally during generation.
Methodology examines only the residual stream, leaving attention patterns and MLP internals as areas for future investigation.
future_direction: Causal intervention studies to validate whether the cognitive representations are functionally utilized by the model.
Cross-lingual and cross-domain analysis to establish universality of the findings.
Investigating attention patterns and MLP internals.
papers.abstract: The black-box nature of Large Language Models necessitates novel evaluation frameworks that transcend surface-level performance metrics. This study investigates the internal neural representations of cognitive complexity using Bloom's Taxonomy as a hierarchical lens. By analyzing high-dimensional activation vectors from different LLMs, we probe whether different cognitive levels, ranging from basic recall (Remember) to abstract synthesis (Create), are linearly separable within the model's residual streams. Our results demonstrate that linear classifiers achieve approximately 95% mean accuracy across all Bloom levels, providing strong evidence that cognitive level is encoded in a linearly accessible subspace of the model's representations. These findings provide evidence that the model resolves the cognitive difficulty of a prompt early in the forward pass, with representations becoming increasingly separable across layers.

papers.title: Do Natural Language Descriptions of Model Activations Convey Privileged Information?
papers.research_question: Do natural language descriptions of model activations (verbalization) provide privileged knowledge about the target model's internals, or do they mainly convey input information and the verbalizer's own knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that existing verbalization methods often do not convey privileged knowledge about the target model's internals, but instead reflect input information or the verbalizer's own knowledge, highlighting the need for better benchmarks and controls.
papers.conclusion: The results indicate a need for targeted benchmarks and experimental controls to rigorously assess whether verbalization methods provide meaningful insights into the operations of LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
For feature extraction datasets, a zero-shot baseline achieves high accuracy without access to activations, suggesting privileged knowledge may not be necessary for verbalization to succeed.
Prediction on reconstructed text (via inversion) matches verbalization performance, indicating tasks may elicit input text information rather than privileged knowledge.
Verbalizers often rely on their own world knowledge, especially when there is a mismatch between target and verbalizer knowledge, as shown in PersonaQA experiments.
Verbalization is sensitive to prompt phrasing, complicating interpretation of verbalizer outputs.
future_direction: Developing better benchmarks and experimental controls to assess verbalization methods.
papers.abstract: Recent interpretability methods have proposed to translate LLM internal representations into natural language descriptions using a second verbalizer LLM. This is intended to illuminate how the target model represents and operates on inputs. But do such activation verbalization approaches actually provide privileged knowledge about the internal workings of the target model, or do they merely convey information about its inputs? We critically evaluate popular verbalization methods across datasets used in prior work and find that they can succeed at benchmarks without any access to target model internals, suggesting that these datasets may not be ideal for evaluating verbalization methods. We then run controlled experiments which reveal that verbalizations often reflect the parametric knowledge of the verbalizer LLM which generated them, rather than the knowledge of the target LLM whose activations are decoded. Taken together, our results indicate a need for targeted benchmarks and experimental controls to rigorously assess whether verbalization methods provide meaningful insights into the operations of LLMs.

papers.title: Can LLMs Predict Their Own Failures? Self-Awareness via Internal Circuits
papers.research_question: Can LLMs predict their own failures by inspecting internal states during inference?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Gnosis, a lightweight self-awareness mechanism that enables frozen LLMs to perform intrinsic self-verification by decoding signals from hidden states and attention patterns with negligible inference overhead.
papers.conclusion: Gnosis provides a highly efficient framework for self-evaluation and sibling modeling, enabling early error detection and compute-aware control, demonstrating that intrinsic self-verification is both scalable and cost-effective.
papers.key_findings:
Gnosis consistently outperforms strong internal baselines and large external judges (e.g., 8B reward models, Gemini 2.5 Pro) in accuracy and calibration across math reasoning, QA, and academic knowledge benchmarks.
Gnosis generalizes zero-shot to partial generations, enabling early detection of failing trajectories and compute-aware control.
A Gnosis head trained on a small backbone transfers effectively to judge larger sibling models without fine-tuning.
Gnosis adds only ~5M parameters and operates with negligible inference cost, independent of sequence length.
Results show that reliable correctness cues are intrinsic to the generation process and can be extracted efficiently without external supervision.
papers.limitation: Gnosis is designed as a self-awareness mechanism rather than a general-purpose reward model; it transfers robustly to siblings but is not capable of acting as a general reward model.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) generate fluent and complex outputs but often fail to recognize their own mistakes and hallucinations. Existing approaches typically rely on external judges, multi-sample consistency, or text-based self-critique, which incur additional compute or correlate weakly with true correctness. We ask: can LLMs predict their own failures by inspecting internal states during inference? We introduce Gnosis, a lightweight self-awareness mechanism that enables frozen LLMs to perform intrinsic self-verification by decoding signals from hidden states and attention patterns. Gnosis passively observes internal traces, compresses them into fixed-budget descriptors, and predicts correctness with negligible inference cost, adding only ~5M parameters and operating independently of sequence length. Across math reasoning, open-domain question answering, and academic knowledge benchmarks, and over frozen backbones ranging from 1.7B to 20B parameters, Gnosis consistently outperforms strong internal baselines and large external judges in both accuracy and calibration. Moreover, it generalizes zero-shot to partial generations, enabling early detection of failing trajectories and compute-aware control. These results show that reliable correctness cues are intrinsic to generation process and can be extracted efficiently without external supervision.

papers.title: SCIURus: Shared Circuits for Interpretable Uncertainty Representations in Language Models
papers.research_question: Do the factuality of generated responses and a model's uncertainty originate in separate or shared circuits within the model architecture?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides strong evidence that a language model's uncertainty and the factuality of its generated answers are produced by shared circuits in the model, rather than separate ones.
papers.conclusion: The results broadly support the shared circuits hypothesis, suggesting that P(IK) probing elicits introspective, interpretable uncertainty estimates and that uncertainty quantification in LLMs may largely rely on the same circuitry used for question-answering.
papers.key_findings:
Causal tracing experiments show that the same model components (layers, attention heads) affect both the model's correct-token probability and the P(IK) probe's confidence estimate.
Zero-ablation experiments (both leave-one-out and COAR) across multiple models and datasets support the shared circuits hypothesis, with changes in model accuracy and probe output being highly correlated.
The P(IK) probe's uncertainty representation often remains calibrated even after interventions that damage model performance.
The shared circuits hypothesis holds across a range of models (Llama 2/3, Gemma 2) and datasets (TriviaQA, WebQuestions, MMLU, ARC, CounterFact).
Some discrepancies occur, such as when answer tokens appear in the question, where restorations can suppress model accuracy but not probe confidence.
papers.limitation:
Zero-ablation may lack specificity because zeroing out a component can severely damage general language coherence, not just task-specific information flow.
Causal tracing may miss important circuits when information flows along multiple parallel paths, as restoring a single path may not show a substantial effect.
future_direction: Analyze the mechanisms responsible for P(IK) estimates in greater detail.
Apply P(IK) probing as an interpretability tool to study phenomena like hallucination in LLMs.
Perform similar analyses on other uncertainty quantification methods, such as verbalized uncertainty.
papers.abstract: Carter Teplica, Yixin Liu, Arman Cohan, Tim G. J. Rudner. Proceedings of the 2025 Conference of the Nations of the Americas Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics: Human Language Technologies (Volume 1: Long Papers). 2025.

papers.title: Language Models Can Predict Their Own Behavior
papers.research_question: Can the internal representations of language models predict their eventual behavior before any output token is generated?
papers.core_contribution: Linear probes on the internal representations of input tokens can predict a wide range of eventual behaviors of language models, and when combined with conformal prediction, provide provable bounds on estimation error for precise early warning systems.
papers.conclusion: Internal representations of language models contain information about eventual behavior, and conformal probes can provide reliable early warning systems for various behaviors, enabling efficient and safe deployment.
papers.key_findings:
Probes trained on hidden states of input tokens can predict instruction-following failures with high consistency, outperforming a fine-tuned BERT baseline.
Conformal probes can detect safety alignment failures (jailbreaking) and reduce jailbreak success rate from 30% to 2.7%, a 91% reduction.
Probes can preemptively estimate an LM's confidence as measured by per-token perplexity, a behavior that cannot be inferred from output text alone.
When applied to CoT prompting for text classification, conformal probes reduce inference costs by 65% on average across 27 datasets with negligible accuracy loss.
Probes generalize to unseen datasets and perform better on larger models, suggesting favorable scaling properties.
papers.limitation:
The approach relies on the exchangeability assumption for conformal prediction, which may not hold in practice.
The method was only tested on a few datasets and with a few runs.
papers.abstract: The text produced by language models (LMs) can exhibit specific `behaviors,' such as a failure to follow alignment training, that we hope to detect and react to during deployment. Identifying these behaviors can often only be done post facto, i.e., after the entire text of the output has been generated. We provide evidence that there are times when we can predict how an LM will behave early in computation, before even a single token is generated. We show that probes trained on the internal representation of input tokens alone can predict a wide range of eventual behaviors over the entire output sequence. Using methods from conformal prediction, we provide provable bounds on the estimation error of our probes, creating precise early warning systems for these behaviors. The conformal probes can identify instances that will trigger alignment failures (jailbreaking) and instruction-following failures, without requiring a single token to be generated. An early warning system built on the probes reduces jailbreaking by 91%. Our probes also show promise in pre-emptively estimating how confident the model will be in its response, a behavior that cannot be detected using the output text alone. Conformal probes can preemptively estimate the final prediction of an LM that uses Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting, hence accelerating inference. When applied to an LM that uses CoT to perform text classification, the probes drastically reduce inference costs (65% on average across 27 datasets), with negligible accuracy loss. Encouragingly, probes generalize to unseen datasets and perform better on larger models, suggesting applicability to the largest of models in real-world settings.

papers.title: On the Role of Attention Heads in Large Language Model Safety
papers.research_question: What is the connection between standard attention mechanisms and safety capability in large language models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Ships and Sahara to identify safety-critical attention heads in LLMs, showing that ablating a small number of these heads significantly reduces model safety.
papers.conclusion: Ships and Sahara provide a novel perspective for interpreting safety in LLMs, revealing that specific attention heads are crucial for safety and are sparsely distributed.
papers.key_findings:
Safety attention heads are sparse; ablating them significantly increases the attack success rate (ASR).
Safety heads primarily function as feature extractors for safety.
Models fine-tuned from the same base model exhibit overlapping safety heads.
Ablating safety heads has minimal impact on model helpfulness.
The proposed method localizes safety parameters at a finer granularity (head-level) compared to prior work.
future_direction: Exploring the association between attention heads and other safety capabilities beyond direct rejection.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) achieve state-of-the-art performance on multiple language tasks, yet their safety guardrails can be circumvented, leading to harmful generations. In light of this, recent research on safety mechanisms has emerged, revealing that when safety representations or component are suppressed, the safety capability of LLMs are compromised. However, existing research tends to overlook the safety impact of multi-head attention mechanisms, despite their crucial role in various model functionalities. Hence, in this paper, we aim to explore the connection between standard attention mechanisms and safety capability to fill this gap in the safety-related mechanistic interpretability. We propose a novel metric which tailored for multi-head attention, the Safety Head ImPortant Score (Ships), to assess the individual heads' contributions to model safety. Based on this, we generalize Ships to the dataset level and further introduce the Safety Attention Head AttRibution Algorithm (Sahara) to attribute the critical safety attention heads inside the model. Our findings show that the special attention head has a significant impact on safety. Ablating a single safety head allows aligned model (e.g., Llama-2-7b-chat) to respond to 16 times more harmful queries, while only modifying 0.006% of the parameters, in contrast to the ~ 5% modification required in previous studies. More importantly, we demonstrate that attention heads primarily function as feature extractors for safety and models fine-tuned from the same base model exhibit overlapping safety heads through comprehensive experiments. Together, our attribution approach and findings provide a novel perspective for unpacking the black box of safety mechanisms within large models.

papers.title: Beyond Words: A Latent Memory Approach to Internal Reasoning in LLMs
papers.research_question: Can incorporating implicit mental representations (latent memory) into LLMs lead to more efficient internal reasoning compared to explicit chain-of-thought reasoning?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a framework that integrates an Implicit Memory Module (IMM) into LLMs to enhance internal reasoning efficiency using latent representations, demonstrating reduced training loss compared to a baseline model.
papers.conclusion: The Implicit Memory Module framework improves model efficiency for internal reasoning, and future work can explore integrating explicit interpretability channels without compromising computational gains.
papers.key_findings:
Incorporating the IMM into a GPT model reduced final training loss by 35% to 57% across different context window sizes.
The IMM is designed to be computationally efficient and scalable, with overhead that is minimal compared to standard transformer operations.
The framework allows for optional integration of an explicit chain-of-thought decoder for interpretability without burdening the core inference process.
Preliminary experiments on adaptive long-term memory during inference revealed challenges including increased computational cost, stability issues, and security risks.
papers.limitation:
Preliminary experiments were conducted on a small dataset (Shakespeare) with limited context windows.
Attempts at adaptive long-term memory during inference increased computational costs, introduced stability issues like catastrophic forgetting, and posed potential security risks.
future_direction: Explore safer and more effective methods to incorporate explicit auditability without compromising computational efficiency, such as lightweight chain-of-thought decoders.
Conduct further theoretical analysis and ablation studies, such as varying the number of memory slots and testing different summarization strategies.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have popularized the chain-of-thought (CoT) paradigm, in which models produce explicit reasoning steps in natural language. Although this approach improves interpretability and facilitates external auditing, it may not represent the most computationally efficient method for internal reasoning. In contrast, human cognition relies on implicit mental representations that recall past sensory and episodic information without requiring complete verbalization. In this paper, we propose a framework that integrates implicit mental representations into the internal reasoning processes of LLMs. Preliminary experiments indicate that incorporating an Implicit Memory Module (IMM) into a simple GPT model yields a reduction of between 35% and 57% in final training loss compared to a regular GPT baseline. The addition of an explicit interpretability channel (e.g., a chain-of-thought decoder) is straightforward to implement within this approach. We outline theoretical foundations, propose technical mechanisms to scale the memory module, and discuss how these ideas may lead to more efficient and robust reasoning, with optional future extensions for explicit auditability.

papers.title: Knowing Before Saying: LLM Representations Encode Information About Chain-of-Thought Success Before Completion
papers.research_question: Can the success of a zero-shot Chain-of-Thought process be predicted before completion, and do LLMs encode information about reasoning success in their internal representations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that LLM internal representations encode information about Chain-of-Thought success before generation, and a probing classifier can predict success, enabling potential early stopping.
papers.conclusion: The success of CoT reasoning can be predicted from LLM internal representations before generation, and these findings may inform methods to make CoT more efficient without sacrificing performance.
papers.key_findings:
A probing classifier based on LLM internal representations can predict CoT success before any token generation with 60% to 76.4% accuracy.
Internal representations outperform a BERT baseline that relies on generated tokens, indicating they encode deeper reasoning dynamics.
Providing later reasoning steps does not always improve prediction accuracy, and when it doesn't, earlier representations are more similar to later ones.
Early stopping experiments show that truncating CoT reasoning still improves performance over not using CoT, though a gap remains compared to full reasoning.
The model's intermediate representations may encode sufficient information for correct answers, but zero-shot early stopping is suboptimal.
papers.limitation:
The test set for Mistral-7B was annotated by GPT-4o mini, which may be less reliable than human annotation, and results should be interpreted with caution.
Zero-shot early stopping is a suboptimal intervention because the model does not always converge to a stable answer even when nearly the entire reasoning sequence is generated.
future_direction: Using supervised learning to train the model to generate concise reasoning chains.
Using reinforcement learning to reinforce brevity via rewards.
papers.abstract: We investigate whether the success of a zeroshot Chain-of-Thought (CoT) process can be predicted before completion.We discover that a probing classifier, based on LLM representations, performs well even before a single token is generated, suggesting that crucial information about the reasoning process is already present in the initial steps representations.In contrast, a strong BERT-based baseline, which relies solely on the generated tokens, performs worse-likely because it depends on shallow linguistic cues rather than deeper reasoning dynamics.Surprisingly, using later reasoning steps does not always improve classification.When additional context is unhelpful, earlier representations resemble later ones more, suggesting LLMs encode key information early.This implies reasoning can often stop early without loss.To test this, we conduct early stopping experiments, showing that truncating CoT reasoning still improves performance over not using CoT at all, though a gap remains compared to full reasoning.However, approaches like supervised learning or reinforcement learning designed to shorten CoT chains could leverage our classifier's guidance to identify when early stopping is effective.Our findings provide insights that may support such methods, helping to optimize CoT's efficiency while preserving its benefits.

papers.title: Two Pathways to Truthfulness: On the Intrinsic Encoding of LLM Hallucinations
papers.research_question: How do truthfulness cues arise and function within LLMs?
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers two distinct internal pathways (Question-Anchored and Answer-Anchored) for truthfulness encoding in LLMs and leverages this understanding to improve hallucination detection.
papers.conclusion: The work provides new insights into how LLMs internally encode truthfulness, offering directions for building more reliable and self-aware generative systems.
papers.key_findings:
Truthfulness signals in LLMs arise from two distinct information pathways: a Question-Anchored pathway dependent on question-answer flow, and an Answer-Anchored pathway derived from the generated answer itself.
The two pathways are associated with the model's knowledge boundaries: Q-Anchored encoding predominates for well-known facts, while A-Anchored encoding is favored for long-tail cases.
LLMs exhibit intrinsic self-awareness, as their internal representations can distinguish which truthfulness encoding pathway is being employed.
The proposed pathway-aware detection methods, Mixture-of-Probes (MoP) and Pathway Reweighting (PR), consistently improve hallucination detection performance across diverse datasets and models.
papers.abstract: Despite their impressive capabilities, large language models (LLMs) frequently generate hallucinations. Previous work shows that their internal states encode rich signals of truthfulness, yet the origins and mechanisms of these signals remain unclear. In this paper, we demonstrate that truthfulness cues arise from two distinct information pathways: (1) a Question-Anchored pathway that depends on question-answer information flow, and (2) an Answer-Anchored pathway that derives self-contained evidence from the generated answer itself. First, we validate and disentangle these pathways through attention knockout and token patching. Afterwards, we uncover notable and intriguing properties of these two mechanisms. Further experiments reveal that (1) the two mechanisms are closely associated with LLM knowledge boundaries; and (2) internal representations are aware of their distinctions. Finally, building on these insightful findings, two applications are proposed to enhance hallucination detection performance. Overall, our work provides new insight into how LLMs internally encode truthfulness, offering directions for more reliable and self-aware generative systems.

papers.title: The Geometry of Truth: Emergent Linear Structure in Large Language Model Representations of True/False Datasets
papers.research_question: Do large language models (LLMs) linearly represent the truth or falsehood of factual statements in their internal representations?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides evidence that at sufficient scale, LLMs compute and linearly represent the truth of factual statements in their internal activations, and introduces mass-mean probing as a simple method that identifies directions more causally implicated in model outputs.
papers.conclusion: The work finds evidence that LLMs linearly represent truth at scale, localizes these representations to specific hidden states, and shows that mass-mean probing is an effective method for identifying causally implicated truth directions.
papers.key_findings:
Linear representations of truth emerge with model scale, with larger models developing a more abstract notion of truth applicable across diverse inputs.
Truth representations are localized to a small group of hidden states (over the end-of-sentence punctuation token) in the residual stream.
Simple difference-in-mean (mass-mean) probes generalize as well as other probing techniques (logistic regression, CCS) for larger models and identify directions that are more causally effective in intervention experiments.
Training probes on datasets that include statements and their logical opposites (e.g., cities and neg cities) improves generalization, mitigating the effect of non-truth correlated features.
Probes trained solely on text likelihood (the likely dataset) perform poorly on datasets where truth and probability are anti-correlated, indicating the represented feature is not merely text probability.
papers.limitation:
Focuses on simple, uncontroversial factual statements, so cannot disambiguate truth from closely related features like 'commonly believed' or 'verifiable'.
Studies only models in the LLaMA-2 family, so results may not generalize to all LLMs.
future_direction: Why were interventions with mass-mean probe directions extracted from the likely dataset effective, despite these probes being inaccurate at classification?
Why did mass-mean probing with the cities+neg_cities training data perform poorly for the 70B model, while mass-mean probing with larger_than+smaller_than performed well?
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have impressive capabilities, but are prone to outputting falsehoods. Recent work has developed techniques for inferring whether a LLM is telling the truth by training probes on the LLM's internal activations. However, this line of work is controversial, with some authors pointing out failures of these probes to generalize in basic ways, among other conceptual issues. In this work, we use high-quality datasets of simple true/false statements to study in detail the structure of LLM representations of truth, drawing on three lines of evidence: 1. Visualizations of LLM true/false statement representations, which reveal clear linear structure. 2. Transfer experiments in which probes trained on one dataset generalize to different datasets. 3. Causal evidence obtained by surgically intervening in a LLM's forward pass, causing it to treat false statements as true and vice versa. Overall, we present evidence that at sufficient scale, LLMs linearly represent the truth or falsehood of factual statements. We also show that simple difference-in-mean probes generalize as well as other probing techniques while identifying directions which are more causally implicated in model outputs.

papers.title: The Side Effects of Being Smart: Safety Risks in MLLMs' Multi-Image Reasoning
papers.research_question: Do improved capabilities in multi-image reasoning expand the attack surface and introduce new safety risks in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs)?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces MIR-SafetyBench, the first benchmark for evaluating multi-image reasoning safety in MLLMs, and finds that models with stronger multi-image reasoning capabilities are often more vulnerable to safety attacks, with unsafe generations exhibiting lower attention entropy.
papers.conclusion: The paper introduces MIR-SafetyBench and demonstrates extensive safety risks in MLLMs during multi-image reasoning, highlighting the need for improved safety alignment in complex multimodal scenarios.
papers.key_findings:
Multi-image relational attacks succeed widely across 19 MLLMs, with the highest Attack Success Rate (ASR) reaching 87.63%.
Within a broad range of models, stronger multi-image reasoning capability correlates with higher ASR, indicating a capability-safety trade-off.
Many safe responses are superficial, arising from misunderstanding, generic refusals, or evasive answers rather than robust safety alignment.
In multi-image scenarios, unsafe generations exhibit lower attention entropy than safe ones on average, suggesting models may over-focus on task solving while neglecting safety constraints.
Multi-image relational prompts lead to significantly higher ASR compared to single-image prompts for the same harmful intent.
papers.limitation:
Benchmark coverage is not exhaustive and may inherit biases from source datasets and the automated pipeline.
Dependence on automatic components (e.g., DeepSeek-R1, FLUX.1-dev, HarmBench classifier) may introduce systematic noise.
Evaluation is limited to a fixed set of models under single-turn prompting, and attention-entropy analysis provides only correlational evidence.
The work is diagnostic rather than prescriptive, with no concrete mitigation mechanisms proposed.
future_direction: Extend MIR-SafetyBench to more realistic user interactions, additional modalities and relation types, and richer measurements of internal states and real-world safety impact.
Bridge the gap from characterization to practical mitigation with detection mechanisms, safety monitors, or training-time regularizers.
papers.abstract: As Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) acquire stronger reasoning capabilities to handle complex, multi-image instructions, this advancement may pose new safety risks. We study this problem by introducing MIR-SafetyBench, the first benchmark focused on multi-image reasoning safety, which consists of 2,676 instances across a taxonomy of 9 multi-image relations. Our extensive evaluations on 19 MLLMs reveal a troubling trend: models with more advanced multi-image reasoning can be more vulnerable on MIR-SafetyBench. Beyond attack success rates, we find that many responses labeled as safe are superficial, often driven by misunderstanding or evasive, non-committal replies. We further observe that unsafe generations exhibit lower attention entropy than safe ones on average. This internal signature suggests a possible risk that models may over-focus on task solving while neglecting safety constraints. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/thu-coai/MIR-SafetyBench.

papers.title: Language Models Represent Space and Time
papers.research_question: Do large language models learn coherent linear representations of space and time, i.e., do they form a world model?
papers.core_contribution: Large language models learn linear representations of space and time that are robust to prompting and unified across entity types, and individual 'space' and 'time' neurons exist that encode these coordinates.
papers.conclusion: Modern LLMs learn rich spatiotemporal representations of the real world and possess basic ingredients of a world model.
papers.key_findings:
Linear probes can recover spatial and temporal coordinates from internal activations, with performance increasing with model size and plateauing in middle layers.
Spatial and temporal features are linearly represented, as nonlinear probes do not improve performance.
Representations are robust to variations in prompting, though random tokens or capitalization degrade performance.
Probes generalize across entity types and to held-out geographic or temporal blocks, indicating unified representations.
Individual neurons exist that are highly predictive of space and time, and causal interventions confirm their importance.
papers.limitation:
Data comes only from English Wikipedia, skewing towards the Anglosphere, and entity type distribution is not uniform.
The true extent and structure of spatial and temporal representations remain unclear.
future_direction: Extracting representations in the model’s coordinate system rather than human coordinates, e.g., with sparse autoencoders.
Studying how these spatiotemporal representations are learned, recalled, and used internally across training checkpoints.
Investigating potential parallels with biological place and grid cells in the brain.
